ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram shows three separate coins. On their visible top faces, each coin has a small paper label: one is numbered 6, one is numbered 7, and one is numbered 8. These are the three numbers that were on top after the first throw and then coloured red. Reasoning: The first-throw top sum is 6 + 7 + 8 = 21. The six numbers are consecutive and include 6, 7, and 8, so the possible blocks of six consecutive numbers are 3–8, 4–9, 5–10, or 6–11. The three still-white numbers are the numbers in the block other than 6, 7, and 8. In later throws, each coin can show either its red-side number or the opposite white-side number. Test the blocks: For 3–8, the white numbers are 3, 4, 5, all smaller than 6, 7, 8, so a later top sum cannot increase from 21 to 23. For 6–11, the white numbers are 9, 10, 11, all larger, so a later top sum cannot decrease from 21 to 17. For 5–10, the white numbers are 5, 9, 10; there is only one smaller white number, 5, and replacing even 8 by 5 lowers 21 only to 18, not 17. For 4–9, the white numbers are 4, 5, 9. This works: if 4 is opposite 8, replacing 8 by 4 gives 6 + 7 + 4 = 17; if 9 is opposite 7, replacing 7 by 9 gives 6 + 9 + 8 = 23. Therefore the three white numbers are 4, 5, and 9, and their sum is 4 + 5 + 9 = 18.

For each block, the three non-red white numbers are the numbers in the block other than 6, 7, 8. A later throw is obtained by choosing, for each coin, either its red-side number or its opposite white-side number, so the later sums must be reachable from 21 by replacing some of 6, 7, 8 with their opposite numbers. Test the blocks: 3–8 cannot reach 23 because all white numbers are smaller; 6–11 cannot reach 17 because all white numbers are larger; 5–10 has only one smaller white number, 5, and even opposite 8 it lowers the sum by only 3, so it cannot reach 17; 4–9 works, for example with 4 opposite 8 giving 17 and 9 opposite 7 giving 23. Therefore the white numbers are 4, 5, and 9, whose sum is 18.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram first: the three coins have top papers 6, 7, and 8, which the text identifies as the red-coloured papers after the first throw. Let the unknown white numbers opposite 6, 7, and 8 be a, b, c in some order. The first visible sum is 6+7+8=21. The second throw sum 23 means some subset of the three coins changed sides and caused a net change of +2; the third throw sum 17 means some subset caused a net change of -4. Thus among the three differences (white number minus its opposite red number), subset sums must include +2 and -4. Because both a positive and a negative net change are needed, the remaining white numbers cannot all lie below 6,7,8 or all above them; this eliminates consecutive blocks 3–8 and 6–11. The only mixed possibilities are whites {4,5,9} from block 4–9 or whites {5,9,10} from block 5–10. In {5,9,10}, there is only one number below the red values, and its largest possible negative difference is 5−8=-3, so a subset sum of -4 is impossible. Hence the whites must be {4,5,9}. Check consistency by pairing 4 opposite 8 for the -4 throw and 9 opposite 7 for the +2 throw. Their sum is 4+5+9=18.

因此三张白色纸片上的数字之和为 4+5+9=18。

He stuck those six pieces of paper on the front and back of three coins. Then he threw the coins three times. After the first throw the numbers 6, 7, 8 were on top (see diagram), which Jakob then coloured in red. After the second throw the sum of the numbers on top was 23 and after the third throw the sum was 17. How big is the sum of the numbers on the three white pieces of paper?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The attached diagram shows three separate coins. On their visible top faces, each coin has a small paper label: one is numbered 6, one is numbered 7, and one is numbered 8. These are the three numbers that were on top after the first throw and then coloured red.

Reasoning: The first-throw top sum is 6 + 7 + 8 = 21. The six numbers are consecutive and include 6, 7, and 8, so the possible blocks of six consecutive numbers are 3–8, 4–9, 5–10, or 6–11. The three still-white numbers are the numbers in the block other than 6, 7, and 8. In later throws, each coin can show either its red-side number or the opposite white-side number.

Test the blocks: For 3–8, the white numbers are 3, 4, 5, all smaller than 6, 7, 8, so a later top sum cannot increase from 21 to 23. For 6–11, the white numbers are 9, 10, 11, all larger, so a later top sum cannot decrease from 21 to 17. For 5–10, the white numbers are 5, 9, 10; there is only one smaller white number, 5, and replacing even 8 by 5 lowers 21 only to 18, not 17. For 4–9, the white numbers are 4, 5, 9. This works: if 4 is opposite 8, replacing 8 by 4 gives 6 + 7 + 4 = 17; if 9 is opposite 7, replacing 7 by 9 gives 6 + 9 + 8 = 23. Therefore the three white numbers are 4, 5, and 9, and their sum is 4 + 5 + 9 = 18.
